note: Focuses on enforcement capacity rather than drafting, on the argument that regulation without enforcement is nothing, and recommends a model for coordinating supranational and national bodies.
title: A Robust Governance for the AI Act: AI Office, AI Board, Scientific Panel, and National Authorities
explain_beginner: The European Union created new rules for artificial intelligence, but having rules means nothing if nobody enforces them. This paper examines who is responsible for making sure companies follow these AI rules and proposes a better system for coordination. The authors explain how different European institutions and national governments should work together to monitor AI companies and ensure everyone follows the same standards fairly.
explain_business: The AI Act requires robust enforcement to be effective, and this paper clarifies the governance structure organizations must navigate. Companies need to understand which European bodies and national authorities will oversee compliance, as implementation varies across member states. The proposed coordination model indicates businesses should expect consistent regulatory standards, but compliance strategies must account for both EU-level oversight and national authority involvement in enforcement actions.
explain_practitioner: The authors analyzed the enforcement mechanisms of the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act across institutional bodies including the European Commission, the newly created AI Office, and national authorities. They mapped roles and responsibilities at both supranational and national levels, examining how regulatory requirements shape institutional capacity and structure. The paper proposes a coordinated governance model designed to achieve consistent implementation and enforcement of the AIA across member states, addressing the administrative and operational requirements necessary for effective regulation execution.
